claims.proposition_evaluated: The City of Edmonton has removed motor-vehicle through lanes for bike lanes across a geographically broad share of Edmonton: under the brief's primary threshold, qualifying corridors in at least 8 of the 15 district-plan areas (alternative threshold: at least 5), as of 2026-09-23.
claims.interpretation_notes: Final position: Partially supported, unchanged. I reach the same row as both gpt reviewers but on a different verified set, not to match them. Verified qualifying corridors, all from City records: (1) 102 Avenue, 121–112 Street at minimum, and 121–111 Street by gpt's reading of the 2017 fact sheet. Built 2017, two-way roadway converted to one-way eastbound with a north-side two-way cycle track. Central district. (2) 83 Avenue, 106–99 Street excluding 102–104 Street. Built 2016–2017, two-way local roadway converted to eastbound-only with protected lanes. Scona district. (3) 100 Street, 83–80 Avenue. Opened 2025, converted to one-way northbound for a two-way protected lane. Scona district. So C is at least 3 and A is at least 2, a verified minimum on an incomplete census (R < T). This is below both 8 and 5, so the row is Partially supported under both thresholds. 132 Avenue probably qualifies for some sections: the City says some sections had four lanes and the renewal sets one driving lane each way with separated bike lanes, and 72 built protected features sit on 132 AVENUE NW in the live layer. I have not matched the built sections to the former four-lane sections in a City drawing, so I do not add it to C. If it were added, A would rise to 3 at most, since 132 Avenue from 127 Street to Fort Road runs through the north-side districts (probably Northwest; I found no City listing for Killarney or Glengarry). Adding it could not reach 5, so the row would not change. In individual inventory features (reviewer's calculation from the live layer, matched by street name and construction year, not by geometry), about 12 protected-lane features clearly sit on verified segments: 102 AVENUE NW 2017 (7), 83 AVENUE NW 2017 (3), 100 STREET NW Constructed 2025 (3). They lie in the same two districts, so the feature unit does not change the classification. Named examples: 102 Avenue 121–111 Street occurred as described, with the bike route as the stated reason. For 102 Avenue east of 109 Street, the downtown 2016 cycle track and the Valley Line LRT were designed together, and the City attributes the 107–102 Street one-lane configuration to the LRT (by other reviewers' reading). A through-lane loss caused by the bike lane is not established there. On 132 Avenue, lanes were reduced from four to two where four existed, and the City states the reasons as traffic calming and fitting a residential collector, with bike lanes in the freed space. That reason is a qualification and does not carry the verdict. This finding says nothing about congestion. Non-material framing note: the brief's corridor unit treats 132 Avenue as one project corridor although prior lane use varies by section. Counting it at corridor level would overstate the qualifying length; it would not change the district count.

claims.suggested_one_line: City records show through lanes removed for bike lanes on parts of 102 Avenue, 83 Avenue and 100 Street, and probably parts of 132 Avenue, but this review verified them in only two of Edmonton's 15 districts, not 'all throughout the city'.
claims.suggested_short_answer: Yes, in places. The City converted 102 Avenue (121–112 Street) in Oliver, and 83 Avenue and 100 Street in Strathcona, from two-way to one-way streets to fit protected bike lanes. On 132 Avenue it is cutting four-lane sections to one lane each way, citing traffic calming. The verified conversions sit in two of 15 districts. The loss of lanes on 102 Avenue downtown is tied up with the LRT. This says nothing about whether congestion changed.
